# Introduction

The Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) estimator can serve as a powerful inferential
tool. These notes examine the statistical properties that make OLS valuable for
drawing inferences about population parameters from sample data.

# The Regression Function

We start from a model of the form
$$y_i = \mathbf{x}'_i\boldsymbol{\beta} + \varepsilon_i,$$
or in matrix form $\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta} + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$.

A key property of $\varepsilon$ is its orthogonality to all $\mathbf{x}_i$:
$$E[\mathbf{x}_i \cdot \varepsilon_i] = \mathbf{0} \quad \forall\, i \in \{1, \ldots, n\}.$$

## Finite-sample assumptions

```{=typst}
#nmu-callout(title: "The Gauss–Markov Assumptions", kind: "note")[
  + *Linearity* — the model is linear in parameters.
  + *Random sampling* — the data are randomly sampled.
  + *No perfect collinearity* among the regressors.
  + *Zero conditional mean* — $E[epsilon_i | bold(X)] = 0$.
  + *Homoskedasticity* — $V[epsilon_i | bold(X)] = sigma^2$ for all $i$.
]
```

Under these assumptions OLS is the Best Linear Unbiased Estimator (BLUE).

```{=typst}
#nmu-callout(title: "Normality not required", kind: "warning")[
  The Gauss–Markov assumptions make no claim about the distribution of the error
  terms — normality is only needed for exact finite-sample inference.
]
```

# Results

The OLS estimator $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{y}$
is unbiased and has covariance $\sigma^2 (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}$.

```{=typst}
#nmu-callout(title: "Key result", kind: "tip")[
  Among all linear unbiased estimators, OLS attains the smallest variance.
]
```

Native Quarto callouts are also restyled in the NMU palette, and — unlike the
`{=typst}` boxes above — can contain executable code cells, Markdown and
cross-references:

::: {.callout-note title="Estimating the variance"}
The error variance $\sigma^2$ is estimated by
$s^2 = \dfrac{\hat{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}'\hat{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}}{n - k}$,
where $k$ is the number of regressors (including the intercept).
:::
